fallback_summary_en: Languages organize nouns and agreement in very different ways. Some have no grammatical noun gender, some have two or three genders, and some use larger noun-class systems. Articles can make gender visible, but article count is not the same thing as gender count.

transparency_slide.description: The lesson is declarative structure layered with language data. It compares grammatical gender systems without assuming every language has gender, articles, or a masculine/feminine/neuter three-way split.
transparency_slide.rendering_model: Render profile/session languages first using their own comparison records. Comparison records describe the grammatical system and provide representative display forms; they never derive gender count from article count. For an English-to-Spanish session, English supplies the zero-gender contrast and Spanish the two-gender target; Greek is the preferred display-only reference anchor when a three-gender contrast is useful. A reference anchor never gains profile or practice status.

support_selection.full: Render the language comparison block plus structured rules, reviewed examples, and defensible practice for this language.
support_selection.comparison_only: Render the language comparison block only. Do not synthesize missing agreement rules or practice.
support_selection.unavailable: Omit the language from this lesson until a reviewed comparison record exists.

title_policy.notes: The title names the grammatical concept, not a guessed article equivalent. Languages without articles or grammatical gender still fit the same lesson family.

eligibility.notes: The data model supports no-gender, two-gender, three-gender, and larger noun-class systems. Greek may be used as a display-only three-gender reference anchor when it adds useful contrast.

block_plan.notes: Introduce grammatical gender as a noun/agreement system. Explicitly distinguish grammatical gender from a person's gender and from biological sex.

For each ordered language, show the language label and representative forms from its comparison record. The comparison blurb explains whether the language has no grammatical noun gender, two genders, three genders, or a broader noun-class system. Article forms are examples, not the definition of gender.
Explain that gender may be visible on articles, adjectives, pronouns, numerals, case forms, or other agreement targets, and some languages have no grammatical gender at all.

For Spanish, teach two noun genders, article/adjective agreement, useful-but-imperfect ending clues, and limited neuter constructions. Never present Spanish neuter forms as a third ordinary noun gender.
Prefer lesson-safe reviewed sentences that make agreement visible. Exact occurrence evidence remains in gef-content.
Transition from identifying the noun's gender to choosing agreement forms. Omit if no full-support learning language is selected.
Use shared cloze/feature primitives. Spanish practice may choose el/la, un/una, or a gender-variable adjective only when the noun and answer are unambiguous.
Offer a reader hunt for noun phrases whose articles/adjectives reveal grammatical gender. Do not ask learners to infer a person's gender from grammar.
Reinforce: learn the noun with its agreement pattern; endings are clues, not laws; neuter behavior differs by language.

learning_path_policy.notes: Spanish can place this early because noun/article agreement is foundational. Other languages need independent placement and may use comparison-only mode.
